L’Escalier, une adresse pour les jeunes: L’Escalier, a Place to Go for Youth in Lachine’s Disadvantaged Neighbourhoods
À Lachine, L’Escalier offre aux jeunes u: In Lachine, L’Escalier gives young people a place to break isolation, build connections, gain confidence and discover new horizons.
‍<strong>À la maison des jeunes L’Escali: ‍At the L’Escalier de Lachine youth centre, the Les Jumelés day camp is winding down. Before heading home, children play together one last time under the watchful eye of the young counsellors. In some of Lachine’s disadvantaged and isolated neighbourhoods, where spaces for youth are scarce, L’Escalier, which will turn 42 in November, is much more than a place for activities for many.
Le soleil joue à cache-cache en ce vendr: The sun is playing hide-and-seek this Friday, August 21. Outside the <l1>L’Escalier de Lachine</l1> youth centre, children are still bustling around a big table, laughing, eating and finishing the summer together, swept along by a DJ’s musical selections.
Vêtus de chandails de couleur orange, de: Wearing orange T-shirts, teenagers trained to lead, supervise and organize the centre’s activities keep a close watch. Some found their first paid job here, while others are taking on responsibility for the first time.
Yohan est de ceux-là. Arrivé du Cameroun: Yohan is one of them. He arrived from Cameroon at age nine and grew up in Duff-Court, in Lachine. Today, at 18, he studies at CEGEP André-Laurendeau and works as a counsellor at L’Escalier. But before becoming one of the people in charge of supervision, he was simply a kid looking for somewhere to go.
<strong>« J’étais à Montréal sans vraime: “I was in Montréal without really being in Montréal”
Yohan a découvert L’Escalier au cours de: Yohan discovered L’Escalier in the summer of 2024, when a friend, Wilfried, brought him there for his birthday. There, he found young people his own age, people who, he says, “look like you,” live some of the same realities and sometimes speak the same language. Noticed for his energy and his ease communicating, he was first recruited as an apprentice cook for the day camp, before going through training and becoming a counsellor. His journey, he says, has above all broadened his horizons. “I was in Montréal without really being in Montréal.” His world was mostly limited to Lachine. Trips with his parents were mainly to get to an appointment or take care of something, rarely to discover the city.
La remarque de Yohan prend aussi place d: Yohan’s remark also comes in a territory undergoing change. While the proportion of immigrants in Lachine remains below the Montréal average, it jumped by 11% from 2016 to 2021, according to Centraide of Greater Montréal, whereas the increase was only 1% for Montréal as a whole over the same period.
C’est grâce à la maison des jeunes que Y: It was thanks to the youth centre that Yohan discovered other places and other possibilities. “Before coming here, I spent maybe six years in Lachine, but I had never explored Montréal,” he says. For him, this openness matters especially when you grow up in a neighbourhood where opportunities aren’t the same for everyone. L’Escalier then also becomes a gateway to a city that young people live in without necessarily knowing it.
Pour M<sup>me</sup> Onomo Lopes, il faut: For Ms<sup>.</sup> Onomo Lopes, we also have to look at the city these young people are growing up in. “Lachine is quite a special place in the way it’s made up,” she says, adding that very different social realities coexist within the same territory. Some areas are better off, while others, like Lachine-Est, Duff-Court and Saint-Pierre, face compounded hardships.
Les particularités de cette géographie s: The particularities of this social geography also show up in the data. According to the <l1>Centraide of Greater Montréal neighbourhood profile</l1>, the low-income rate reaches 20% in Duff-Court and 13% in Saint-Pierre, compared with 10% for Lachine as a whole. Duff-Court also has the highest proportion of single-parent families of any area in Montréal, at 62%.
Les deux secteurs se distinguent aussi p: The two areas also stand out for their diversity. In Duff-Court, 52% of residents belong to a visible minority group, and the proportion reaches 43% in Saint-Pierre. In these neighbourhoods, home to many of the young people met at L’Escalier, the question of an accessible place to gather goes well beyond a simple need for recreation.
Pour Yohan, Duff-Court présente ses prop: For Yohan, Duff-Court has its own difficulties. He describes a neighbourhood where many young people come from immigrant families and where certain situations can quickly become overwhelming for a teenager. The Saint-Pierre area, meanwhile, is marked by its isolation and the limited services available. To take part in certain activities or access certain services, young people have no choice but to take public transit.
Bernard, qui est âgé de 18 ans, décrit S: Bernard, who is 18, describes Saint-Pierre as a neighbourhood “apart,” where places to socialize are rare. Kirkland Park, he says, is practically the only gathering space that comes to mind for young people.
Quand il n’y a pas d’endroit où aller, i: When there’s nowhere to go, what’s left is the street, the park, sports or fast-food restaurants. In an area like Saint-Pierre, where the low-income rate reaches 13% and whose isolation makes it harder to access certain resources, how close things are, how far people have to travel and what families can afford also determine what is really accessible.
Pour certains, disposer d’un endroit où: For some, having a place to go regularly, in an accessible and supervised setting, becomes a resource in itself. Béatrice, who is 17, knows this routine well.
Béatrice a découvert la maison des jeune: Béatrice discovered the youth centre through a teacher at her school, Dalbé-Viau. She was often bored and didn’t know where to go or what to do with her time. “When I arrived [in Quebec], I didn’t have much to do, I was bored all the time,” she confides, adding that it was thanks to L’Escalier that she started discovering museums, movies, cooking workshops and camping, among other things.
Béatrice se décrit comme une personne ti: Béatrice describes herself as shy. And for her, the youth centre has also become a place where she can talk when she’s going through a hard time. “When I have problems, I don’t have anyone around me to talk to,” she says. Here, she knows she can turn to someone and get an answer.
Pour cette jeune qui ne maîtrise pas enc: For this young woman who doesn’t yet speak French perfectly, the place has also become a space to practise and improve through conversations with other young people. Then, little by little, her role changed, and she found herself supervising children younger than she is.
Pour Yohan, le mot qui revient dans son: For Yohan, the word that keeps coming up in his account is simple: new. It could be a cooking activity, an outing, an art project or a place in Montréal he doesn’t know. The youth centre also revived passions in him like drawing, art and music. “It re-inspired me,” he says.
Les jeunes ne sont pas les seuls à obser: Young people aren’t the only ones who see changes. Marlène Beliz Ngala sees them at home, in her daughter Hélène, who has been coming to L’Escalier for two years.
Lorsque la famille est arrivée au Québec: When the family arrived in Quebec about three and a half years ago, Hélène was, according to her mother, much more alone and reserved. “She was really alone. She didn’t want to talk much.”
Aujourd’hui, Marlène la voit prendre con: Today, Marlène sees her gaining confidence. Sometimes she notices it in small things. At home, Hélène had long resisted her mother’s attempts to teach her how to cook. Then, one day, she announced that she wanted to make pasta. Her father had trouble believing she had made it herself. “No, you did not make that!” he said, incredulous.
Marlène estime que sa fille revient déso: Marlène believes her daughter now comes home with a new confidence. “It really gave me joy to send her to the youth centre even more so she could learn a lot,” she says.
Pour la directrice de L’Escalier, ces ex: For L’Escalier’s director, these experiences can’t be taken for granted in newly arrived families, where parents work a lot and are themselves discovering their new environment. Some are unfamiliar with the resources available or hesitate to let their children go out.
Par ailleurs, et comme beaucoup de paren: Also, like many parents, Marlène says she has worries about her teenager. But she trusts the team and L’Escalier’s director, with whom she talks regularly. That trust was built by watching the changes in her daughter.
À l’exception de Lachine-Ouest, tous les: With the exception of Lachine-Ouest, every area of the borough has single-parent family rates above the Montréal average of 33%. In Duff-Court, nearly two out of three families are single-parent.
Ces données, à elles seules, ne disent r: These figures, on their own, say nothing about how parents raise their children. They do remind us, however, that supervising a teenager doesn’t rely on the same resources or the same availability everywhere. In this context, the trust a parent places in a community organization can take on particular importance.
<strong>Quand le jeune devient celui qui: When the young person becomes the one who supervises
Vendredi, Yohan était là, au milieu des: On Friday, Yohan was there, in the middle of the children, whom he now sees in a different light. He recognizes in them that need to try things, to do something that breaks from routine, and to discover a world that isn’t limited to home, the park, the basketball court or the neighbourhood fast-food spot. His own path happened in stages: first he walked into the building, then he got involved. Someone noticed his involvement and gave him a first task, then a job, then responsibilities with younger kids. At L’Escalier, a young person doesn’t necessarily stay in the same place.
Muriel, 13 ans, en est déjà à une autre: Muriel, 13, is already at another stage. She sits on the youth centre’s board of directors and says she has gained confidence since she started coming, notably because she discovered there that her opinion could be heard.
Marilou, qui a le même âge, raconte surt: Marilou, who is the same age, mostly talks about the friendships she has formed there. When she started at a new school, she found young people she had met at L’Escalier.
Pour Muriel et Marilou, le changement ne: For Muriel and Marilou, the change doesn’t yet take the form of a job or a career plan. It starts with confidence, with having friends, being listened to and being able to take part in activities.
<strong>Wilfried, revenir de l’autre côt: Wilfried, coming back from the other side
Wilfried, lui, revient désormais à L’Esc: Wilfried now returns to L’Escalier with a different story. Today a police cadet, he came to know the youth centre at a time when his future was far less certain. He says that, not long after arriving from his native Cameroon, he went through a particularly difficult period because of a family conflict. But fortunately, Wilfried remembers, community workers with the SPVM directed him to L’Escalier. There, he found someone who listened to him, and he stayed.
Se confiant à La Converse, il parle aujo: Speaking to La Converse, he talks about that period today with deep gratitude. The youth centre welcomed him at a time when his life could have gone in other directions. He later lived in a youth shelter and pursued his dream of working in policing. Today, that dream is starting to take shape, but Wilfried hasn’t left L’Escalier behind. This afternoon, he’s back, and the young people recognize him and talk to him. Some ask him questions they wouldn’t necessarily ask the director or another adult.
Il tient à préserver cette proximité, di: He wants to preserve that closeness, he says, because he knows from the inside some of the realities they face. Because he also knows what it means to find someone to talk to. His role has changed: he is no longer the one being supported. Today, he’s the one playing that role.
<strong>Le risque de ne plus avoir d’end: The risk of having nowhere to go
L’Escalier joue aussi un rôle moins faci: L’Escalier also plays a role that is harder to measure: it is there before a crisis happens, when a young person simply wants to get out of the house or doesn’t know what to do with their day. Bernard sums up the problem simply when he describes daily life for young people in his neighbourhood: you can spend your time walking the streets without knowing exactly where to go. He says he himself came to L’Escalier after looking for something other than the repetition of sports, home and the same encounters. “I just walked, and I came to the youth centre,” he says.
Vendredi, alors que le camp se terminait: On Friday, as the camp was ending, several generations of young people crossed paths in the same building: children still playing, teenagers supervising them and alumni like Wilfried, who came back to keep a connection with those following in their footsteps. These trajectories don’t take shape in a vacuum. On the contrary, they unfold in areas where social hardships are unevenly distributed and where young people don’t all have the same access to resources, activities and the city.
L’Escalier n’apparaît alors pas seulemen: L’Escalier then appears not only as a place that organizes activities, but as a neighbourhood social infrastructure, with concrete effects on its surroundings. It also reveals, by contrast, what is missing when this kind of place doesn’t exist, isn’t accessible or is stifled by a lack of funding – like <l1>those organizations that find themselves at the end of their rope.</l1>
